why.title: The difference between a coach and an ICF credentialed coach.
why.lede: Anyone can call themselves a coach. An ICF credential is evidence of assessed skill, supervised practice and a binding code of ethics — the assurance procurement, HR and legal teams look for.

items.title: Assessed competence
items.desc: Every credential requires demonstrated coaching skill against ICF core competencies, not just attendance on a course.

items.title: Logged practice hours
items.desc: ACC, PCC and MCC each require documented client hours and mentor coaching before the credential is granted.

items.title: Binding code of ethics
items.desc: Credentialed coaches commit to the ICF Code of Ethics with an independent complaints and review process behind it.

items.title: Ongoing development
items.desc: Credentials are renewed on a three-year cycle with continuing education — competence stays current.

items.title: Four-language reach
items.desc: Coaches working in German, French, Italian and English across every Swiss language region.

items.title: Independent of providers
items.desc: The Switzerland Chapter of ICF is a member association, not a coaching vendor. Our guidance is provider-neutral.

deck.title: What the evidence says about coaching in organisations.
deck.lede: A short walkthrough of the pressures Swiss organisations face and where professional coaching demonstrably moves the needle.

slides.title: Work is being rewritten faster than leaders are being developed.
slides.body: Restructuring, hybrid teams, AI adoption and thinner middle management are landing on the same leaders at once. Traditional training cycles cannot keep pace with the rate of change.
slides.source: The Switzerland Chapter of ICF, organisational briefing 2026

slides.statLabel: of leaders say their development has not kept up with the demands of their role.
slides.body: Capability gaps rarely show up as a training request. They show up as attrition, stalled decisions and teams waiting for direction.

slides.title: Disengagement is expensive, and it compounds quietly.
bullets: Replacing a senior leader typically costs well over a year of salary.
Disengaged teams under-deliver long before anyone resigns.
Poor first-time-manager transitions ripple across every reporting line.
Change fatigue erodes discretionary effort faster than any restructure.

slides.title: Coaching builds thinking capacity, not dependency.
slides.body: A coach does not supply answers. They build the leader's own capacity to read complexity, make decisions under uncertainty and hold difficult conversations — capability that stays in the organisation.

slides.statLabel: of organisations report they recouped at least their investment in coaching.

slides.title: Four moments where coaching pays back fastest.
bullets: Transition into a significantly bigger role.
Leading a team through restructuring or merger.
High-potential talent you cannot afford to lose.
Teams stuck in conflict, silence or avoidance.

slides.title: A coaching culture is a management style, not a budget line.
slides.body: Organisations that train managers in coaching skills change how thousands of everyday conversations run — feedback, delegation, prioritisation and performance discussions all improve at once.

slides.quote: A credential is not a certificate of attendance. It is evidence of assessed, supervised, ethically bound practice.
slides.body: That distinction is why procurement and HR teams increasingly specify ICF credentials in coaching frameworks.

slides.title: Impact you can actually evidence.
bullets: Define outcomes with the sponsor before the first session.
Three-way alignment between coach, coachee and organisation.

slides.title: Start where the pressure is highest.
slides.body: Most organisations begin with a focused pilot: one leadership population, one clear outcome, one measurement window. Scale follows evidence, not enthusiasm.

segments.title: From intergovernmental Geneva to Swiss boardrooms and beyond.
segments.lede: Pick the context closest to yours and we will point to the route and programme most organisations like you start with.

items.label: Intergovernmental (IGO)
items.definition: UN agencies, WHO, WTO, ILO, WEF and the wider international Geneva community.
items.angle: Coaches fluent in multilateral governance, diplomatic complexity and strict neutrality requirements.

items.label: Non-governmental (NGO / INGO)
items.definition: Humanitarian and advocacy organisations, from global INGOs to local associations.
items.angle: Mission-driven leadership under resource constraint, resilience in high-stakes work, coaching for flat or networked structures.

items.label: Governmental (Swiss)

initiatives.title: Three routes into coaching, depending on where you are.

items.title: A focused executive coaching pilot.
items.desc: We help you scope a small, well-measured engagement for a defined leadership population, then match credentialed coaches whose experience fits your sector and language region.

items.title: Team coaching for units under pressure.
items.desc: Whole-team engagements that surface what is unsaid, rebuild trust after change and convert good intentions into agreed working practices.

items.title: Building an internal coaching culture.
items.desc: Programmes that develop coaching skills in your managers, support internal coach pools and set quality standards aligned to ICF competencies and ethics.

survey.title: How mature is coaching in your organisation?
survey.lede: Eight questions, about three minutes. You get an immediate maturity read across four dimensions, and can request a conversation about what to do next.

pressure.question: What is the biggest pressure on your organisation right now?
pressure.hint: Pick the one that feels most true today. It shapes how we read your results.

options.label: Retaining key people
options.insight: Attrition among people you cannot easily replace is usually a leadership-quality signal long before it is a pay signal.

options.label: Leadership capability
options.insight: Leaders promoted for technical strength rarely fail on technique. They struggle with conversations, ambiguity and delegation.

options.label: AI and changing work
options.insight: Technology adoption stalls on human factors — trust, role clarity and the willingness to work differently.

options.label: Inclusion and belonging
options.insight: Inclusion is created or undone in everyday conversations, not in policy documents.

options.label: Cross-team collaboration
options.insight: Silos are usually a symptom of unclear priorities and unspoken conflict rather than bad intent.

scale.label: Often
scale.desc: Common across most of the organisation.

questions.text: Senior leaders visibly model coaching behaviours such as listening, asking and delegating.
Difficult conversations are held early and directly rather than avoided.
Managers have been trained in practical coaching skills, not just performance processes.
People at all levels receive regular, useful developmental feedback.
Coaching is available beyond the executive layer, including to emerging leaders.
People know how to request coaching and what to expect from it.
Coaching engagements start with agreed outcomes and are reviewed against them.
We work with credentialed coaches and hold external providers to a clear quality standard.

emerging.title: Emerging
emerging.desc: Coaching happens occasionally and informally. The fastest gain is a focused pilot with clear outcomes rather than a broad rollout.

developing.title: Developing
developing.desc: The foundations exist but are uneven. Consistency in access, manager capability and measurement will unlock most of the value.

established.title: Established
established.desc: Coaching is a recognised part of how you develop people. The next step is embedding quality standards and widening access.

embedded.title: Embedded
embedded.desc: Coaching is part of your management style. Focus on sustaining quality, supervision and measurable renewal as your organisation changes.
